# heumilkr

<!-- badges: start -->

[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/lschneiderbauer/heumilkr/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/lschneiderbauer/heumilkr/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml) [![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/lschneiderbauer/heumilkr/branch/master/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/lschneiderbauer/heumilkr?branch=master) [![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental) [![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/heumilkr)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=heumilkr) [![python-check](https://github.com/lschneiderbauer/heumilkr/actions/workflows/python-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/lschneiderbauer/heumilkr/actions/workflows/python-check.yaml) [![PyPI status](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/heumilkr)](https://pypi.org/project/heumilkr/)

<!-- badges: end -->

heumilkr provides an implementation of the Clarke-Wright algorithm [@clarke1964] to find a quasi-optimal solution to the [Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_routing_problem). It is available as an R package and as a Python package, which share the same C++ core.

Besides deliveries, it also supports "backhaul": sites with negative demand have goods picked up and brought back to the depot, in any order within a run as long as the load stays within the vehicle capacity.

For a fixed number of vehicle types, the run time grows at best quadratically and at worst cubically with the number of sites $n$. On the problems we tested with randomly placed sites and up to 4000 sites, it grew roughly like $n^{2}$ to $n^{2.1}$, and roughly like $n^{3}$ if a limited vehicle type repeatedly runs out (see [Runtime Benchmarks](#runtime-benchmarks)).

## Installation

### R

You can install the latest CRAN release of heumilkr with:

``` r
install.packages("heumilkr")
```

Alternatively, you can install the development version of heumilkr from [GitHub](https://github.com/) with:

``` r
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("lschneiderbauer/heumilkr")
```

### Python

You can install the latest PyPI release of heumilkr with:

``` sh
pip install heumilkr
```

Alternatively, you can install the development version of heumilkr from [GitHub](https://github.com/), which requires a C++ compiler, with:

``` sh
pip install git+https://github.com/lschneiderbauer/heumilkr
```

The only dependency is NumPy. Install `heumilkr[pandas]` to also get pandas for `Solution.to_pandas()`.

## Example

### R

The following example generates random demands at random locations, defines two vehicle types, applies the Clarke-Wright algorithm to generate quasi-optimal vehicle runs, and shows the resulting vehicle run solution.

```{r example}
library(heumilkr)
set.seed(42)

# generating random demand
demand <- runif(20, 5, 15)

# generating random site positions
positions <-
  data.frame(
    pos_x = c(0, runif(length(demand), -10, 10)),
    pos_y = c(0, runif(length(demand), -10, 10))
  )

solution <-
  clarke_wright(
    demand,
    dist(positions),
    # We have an infinite number of vehicles with capacity 33 available,
    # and two vehicles with capacity 44.
    data.frame(n = c(NA_integer_, 2L), caps = c(33, 44))
  )

print(solution)

# returns the total cost / distance
# (the quantity that is minimized by CVRP)
print(milkr_cost(solution))

# returns the savings resulting from the heuristic optimization procedure
print(milkr_saving(solution))
```

The R package has a built-in plotting function (using [ggplot](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/)) for the result. The individual runs are distinguished by color. The site locations are marked with round circles while the depot is depicted as a square. The line types (solid/dashed/...) are associated to different vehicle types.

```{r example_plot}
plot(solution)
```

### Python

The following example solves a small problem with a fixed set of demands and distances, applies the Clarke-Wright algorithm to generate quasi-optimal vehicle runs, and shows the resulting vehicle run solution.

``` python
import heumilkr as hm

solution = hm.clarke_wright(
    demand=[3, 2, 4, 2],
    # distances between all locations, the first one is the depot
    distances=[
        [0, 1, 1, 2, 3],
        [1, 0, 2, 1, 2],
        [1, 2, 0, 3, 4],
        [2, 1, 3, 0, 1],
        [3, 2, 4, 1, 0],
    ],
    # one vehicle with capacity 6, and an unlimited number with capacity 9
    vehicles=[hm.Vehicle(capacity=6, count=1), hm.Vehicle(capacity=9)],
)

for run in solution.runs:
    print(run)
#> Run(id=0, vehicle=1, sites=(0, 2, 3), loads=(6.0, 2.0, 0.0), distance=6.0, max_load=9.0)
#> Run(id=1, vehicle=0, sites=(1,), loads=(0.0,), distance=2.0, max_load=2.0)

# returns the total cost / distance
# (the quantity that is minimized by CVRP)
print(solution.cost())
#> 8.0

# returns the savings resulting from the heuristic optimization procedure
print(solution.saving())
#> 6.0
```

## How the Algorithm Works

The following animation, made with the R package, shows how the Clarke-Wright algorithm iterates to arrive at its final solution:

```{r, animation.hook="gifski", interval = 0.5, echo = FALSE, results = FALSE}
res <-
  heumilkr:::clarke_wright_stepwise(
    demand,
    dist(positions),
    data.frame(n = c(NA_integer_, 2L), caps = c(33, 44))
  )

lapply(
  res,
  function(sres) {
    plot(sres)
  }
)
```

## Runtime Benchmarks

```{r benchmark_calc, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(bench) # we load that so that the below gets correctly formatted
result <- readRDS(paste0("./benchmark/", readLines("./benchmark/last_result.txt")))

time <- \(n) format(result$median[result$n == n])

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

The benchmarks were taken on an Intel® Xeon® CPU E3-1231 v3 \@ 3.40GHz CPU, through the R package using [bench](https://bench.r-lib.org/). The solver itself is the same C++ code in Python, but converting inputs and results adds some overhead that differs between the two packages.

The following graph shows the run time on one kind of problem: uniformly distributed random sites, demands between 5 and 15 and a vehicle capacity of 33. It amounts to $\sim `r time(110)`$ for $n = 110$, $\sim `r time(1010)`$ for $n = 1010$, and $\sim `r time(1910)`$ for $n = 1910$. Run times can differ for other problems.

```{r benchmark_runtime, echo = FALSE}
result |>
  mutate(
    ymin = as.numeric(mean - std),
    ymax = as.numeric(mean + std),
    median = as.numeric(median)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = median, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "Number of demanding sites",
    labels = scales::label_number(
      scale_cut = scales::cut_long_scale()
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Runtime (in seconds)",
    labels = scales::label_number(
      suffix = "s",
      scale_cut = scales::cut_long_scale()
    )
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  theme_bw()
```

## Documentation

The two packages have separate documentation sites:

-   R package: [website](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/heumilkr/) with the [function reference](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/heumilkr/reference/) and the articles.
-   Python package: [API reference](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/heumilkr/python/).

## Feature Differences

Both packages include the solver with all its options (backhaul, vehicle types and restrictions) and calculate the cost and savings of a solution. The following is only part of the R package:

-   plotting a solution,
-   downloading and solving [CVRPLIB](https://galgos.inf.puc-rio.br/cvrplib/) instances,
-   the [performance vignette](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/heumilkr/articles/clarke_wright_performance.html), although its results also apply to the Python package, since they measure the shared solver.
